anaesthesia.preferred: GA + arterial line (radial + femoral) + large-bore PIV × 2 + 9F introducer with PAC ± TEE (becoming standard of care per ILTS 2024)
considerations: ═══ PRE-OP OPTIMISATION ═══
MELD score for risk stratification; ABO/Rh confirmed; massive transfusion protocol activated; 6–10 units PRBC + FFP + platelets + cryo cross-matched on table

End-stage liver disease physiology: hyperdynamic circulation (high CO, low SVR), cirrhotic cardiomyopathy (latent — unmasked by stress), porto-pulmonary HTN (mPAP > 25 → relative contraindication if > 50), hepatopulmonary syndrome (intrapulmonary shunting), hepato-renal syndrome, hepatic encephalopathy, coagulopathy (rebalanced — both pro- and anti-coagulant factors low), thrombocytopenia, hyponatraemia
Pre-op echo + right heart cath if PHT suspected (porto-pulmonary HTN = critical screening per ILTS 2024)
Avoid pre-op sedation (encephalopathy risk); RSI if active variceal bleeding / ascites / encephalopathy
═══ PHASE 1: PRE-ANHEPATIC (DISSECTION, 2–6 h) ═══

Hyperdynamic baseline (high CO, low SVR) — vasopressor support (noradrenaline 0.05–0.3 mcg/kg/min) often needed; vasopressin 0.01–0.04 U/min (paeds 0.0003–0.001 U/kg/min) helpful for hepatic blood flow + splanchnic perfusion
IVC manipulation → drop in venous return → hypotension; communicate with surgeon, slow positional change

Active bleeding from collaterals, varices, adhesions (especially if previous abdominal surgery e.g. Kasai); ROTEM-guided product replacement (FIBTEM A10 < 10 → fibrinogen 25–50 mg/kg or cryo; EXTEM CT prolonged → PCC 15–25 U/kg or FFP)
Maintain CVP 5–8 mmHg low to reduce venous bleeding (low-CVP strategy) BUT not at expense of MAP < 65 (use vasopressors before fluid)
═══ PHASE 2: ANHEPATIC (IVC CLAMP, 60–120 min) ═══
No hepatic clearance → drug accumulation (avoid morphine, midazolam boluses; use remifentanil, cisatracurium, propofol TCI)
CO drops ~ 50 % from caval clamp (piggyback technique partially preserves IVC flow → less dramatic drop)
Lactic acidosis accumulates (no hepatic lactate clearance); base deficit -10 to -15 typical
Hypothermia accelerates (cold organ, exposure) — fluid warmer mandatory, target ≥ 35.5 °C
Less aggressive transfusion to avoid right heart volume overload at reperfusion (target Hb 7–8, NOT 10)
Methylprednisolone 500–1000 mg IV (adult) / 10 mg/kg (paeds) before unclamping (immunosuppression induction)
PRE-REPERFUSION CHECKLIST (5 min before unclamping — communicate with surgeon):
• K⁺ < 4.0 mEq/L (use insulin/glucose, CaCl₂, NaHCO₃, β2-agonist; consider RRT if refractory)
• Ionised Ca²⁺ > 1.0 mmol/L (CaCl₂ 10 mg/kg or 5–10 mL 10 %)
• Core temp ≥ 35.5 °C
• pH ≥ 7.30 (NaHCO₃ if severe — modest, avoid CO₂ load)
• Vasopressors primed: noradrenaline running, adrenaline bolus 10–100 mcg drawn up, atropine drawn up
• TEE on RV view (acute RV failure expected at reperfusion)
═══ PHASE 3: REPERFUSION (UNCLAMP IVC) — POST-REPERFUSION SYNDROME ═══
Defined: ≥ 30 % drop in MAP within 5 min of unclamping, lasting ≥ 1 min (incidence ~ 30 %)
Pathophysiology: cold, acidotic, hyperkalaemic, potassium- and vasoactive-mediator-rich blood floods RV → acute RV failure + vasoplegia + bradycardia
IMMEDIATE TREATMENT:
• Adrenaline 10–100 mcg IV bolus (titrate to BP) — repeat as needed
• CaCl₂ 5–10 mL 10 % (counters hyperkalaemia + ionotropic)
• Atropine 0.5–1 mg (bradycardia)
• If hyperkalaemia (K⁺ > 6): insulin 10 U + glucose 50 mL 50 %, NaHCO₃ 50 mmol, salbutamol nebuliser

• REFRACTORY: methylene blue 1–2 mg/kg IV over 10 min for vasoplegia (CAUTION: if patient on anti-PAH drugs e.g. sildenafil — drug interactions; AVOID if G6PD deficiency or on SSRIs/MAOIs — serotonin syndrome risk); vasopressin bolus 1–2 U then infusion

• MB-REFRACTORY: hydroxocobalamin 5 g IV over 15 min (per Pai 2024 Clin Transplant — NO scavenging like MB but different binding profile; emerging 2nd-line for vasoplegia, useful if MB contraindicated)
TEE assessment: RV size and function (often dilated, hypokinetic), TR, IVC distension; consider iNO 20–40 ppm if persistent RV dysfunction
═══ PHASE 4: NEOHEPATIC (POST-REPERFUSION, 1–4 h) ═══
Graft function markers: bile production (visible), pH correction, lactate clearance, glucose handling (rising glucose = good sign), coagulation factor production
Coagulation: factor V/VII improve within 30 min if good graft; if persistently abnormal → graft dysfunction
Glucose: monitor q15–30 min; can swing from hypo (no production) to hyper (overshoot + dextrose load) — short-acting insulin titration
Fluid: replace 3rd-space losses (often 5–8 L over case); albumin 5–20 % balanced with crystalloid; avoid Hartmann's after reperfusion (lactate load) — use Plasmalyte/balanced isotonic
Avoid hypocoagulability swinging to hypercoagulability post-graft (HAT — hepatic artery thrombosis risk — communicate with surgeon for low-dose heparin/aspirin per local protocol)
═══ PAEDIATRIC-SPECIFIC ═══
Smaller circulating volume → relatively more transfusion (per kg); rapid hyperkalaemia risk
Pre-reperfusion K⁺ < 4.0 essential (children less tolerant of swings)
Hypocalcaemia more pronounced (immature citrate clearance) — continuous CaCl₂ infusion may be needed
Size-discordant donor liver (large-for-recipient) → more dramatic hypotension at reperfusion (large vessel filling)
Previous Kasai (biliary atresia) → adhesions + dissection bleeding
Glucose lability extreme — q15 min monitoring
Communicate IVC flow with surgeon (direct visualisation)
═══ POST-OP ═══
ICU intubated 6–24 h until graft function confirmed (lactate < 2, bile output, normalising coagulation, conscious wean)
Immunosuppression: methylprednisolone taper + tacrolimus (post-op day 0–1) ± MMF ± basiliximab per centre
Doppler hepatic vessels q12h × 48 h (HAT detection)
Watch for: bleeding, primary non-function (rare, urgent re-transplant), HAT, rejection (later)
NO neuraxial analgesia (coagulopathy persists 48–72 h post-op); use multimodal IV (paracetamol + opioid PCA + ketamine adjunct)

considerations: ═══ PRE-OP ===
Identify high-risk patients for prolonged surgery + blood loss: > 4-level fusion, deformity correction, revision, instrumentation; consider pre-op tranexamic acid + cell salvage availability
Assess for difficult airway (cervical spine pathology — limited extension; congenital deformity); video laryngoscopy + AFOI if needed
Chronic opioid use common — opioid tolerance → consider perioperative ketamine, methadone, multimodal
Frailty score (elderly fusion) — sarcopenia, polypharmacy, anticoagulants
═══ AIRWAY ═══
Cervical pathology: in-line stabilisation, video laryngoscopy (Glidescope / McGrath / Cmac), AFOI if unstable / rheumatoid C1-C2 / severe stenosis
Anterior cervical surgery: post-op airway oedema risk → cuff leak before extubation, dexamethasone, neck swelling monitoring × 24 h
═══ POSITIONING (PRONE — HIGH-RISK) ═══
Eye protection: GENTLE chin tongs + foam pad with cutouts for eyes (Mayfield / Jackson table); document eye check q15 min — POVL (post-operative visual loss) is a sentinel event
Abdomen FREE (avoids raised intra-abdominal pressure → venous engorgement → bleeding); Jackson table preferred over Wilson frame
Pressure points: chest rolls, hips, knees, feet, breasts (women), genitalia (men) — re-check after position
Neck neutral (no rotation); head slightly elevated above heart (improves venous drainage)
Arms: tucked or on arm boards < 90° abduction (avoid brachial plexus stretch)
═══ POVL PREVENTION (POST-OPERATIVE VISUAL LOSS) — CRITICAL ═══
Risk factors per ASA Practice Advisory 2019: long surgery (> 6 h), large blood loss (> 2 L), Wilson frame, obesity, male, diabetes, vascular disease
PREVENTION:
• Head ABOVE heart (avoid head-down)
• Avoid direct eye pressure (q15 min eye checks documented)
• Maintain MAP within 20 % of baseline (avoid prolonged induced hypotension)
• Hb > 9.0 (avoid prolonged severe anaemia)
• Staged surgery if anticipated > 6 h + high blood loss
• Communicate POVL risk in consent for high-risk cases
POVL types: ION (ischaemic optic neuropathy) — commonest in spine, usually bilateral, unrecoverable; CRAO (central retinal artery occlusion) — unilateral, from direct pressure
═══ NEUROMONITORING (SSEP / MEP / EMG) ═══
Indicated for: deformity correction, instrumentation, spinal cord-level surgery, tumours, revisions
REQUIREMENTS: TIVA (propofol + remifentanil — volatile anaesthetics + N₂O depress MEP signals); NO NMB after intubation (use TOF; some centres allow low-dose cisatracurium for SSEP-only monitoring)
Maintain MAP > 80–85 for cord perfusion during instrumentation
SIGNIFICANT SIGNAL CHANGE (> 50 % amplitude drop, > 10 % latency increase) → immediate response:
1. Stop surgery, communicate with surgeon
2. Increase MAP to > 90, Hb > 10, normothermia, normocapnia
3. Surgeon reverses last manoeuvre (loosens distraction, removes pedicle screw)
4. Re-assess at 5 + 10 min
5. If persistent → wake-up test (rare with MEPs) or steroid bolus (controversial post-NASCIS) and abort fixation
═══ BLOOD CONSERVATION ===
TXA mandatory (per multiple RCTs reducing transfusion 30–50 %): adult 15–30 mg/kg load + 1–2 mg/kg/h infusion; paeds 15–30 mg/kg + 10 mg/kg/h (per Coles 2017 systematic review)
Cell salvage routine for > 2-level posterior fusion / deformity correction
Permissive haemodilution (Hb 9–10 acceptable intraop if no ischaemia) — avoid liberal transfusion
Bipolar diathermy + topical haemostatics (Floseal, Surgicel) + warm theatre + correct coagulopathy early
Iron + EPO pre-op for elective major fusion (orthopaedic PBM protocol)
═══ FLUID MANAGEMENT ===
Goal-directed (SVV) — avoid liberal crystalloid (worsens prone-position oedema → ETT/face/airway swelling + abdominal compartment)
Balanced crystalloid (Plasmalyte/Hartmann); albumin 5 % for colloid where needed
═══ ANALGESIA — MULTIMODAL ERAS SPINE ===

PRE-OP: adult — paracetamol 1 g PO + gabapentin 600–900 mg PO single dose (reduces opioid; mind drowsiness in elderly); paediatric/adolescent — paracetamol 15 mg/kg PO + gabapentin 10–15 mg/kg PO (single pre-op dose)
INTRAOP: ketamine 0.15–0.5 mg/kg/h infusion (opioid-sparing + anti-hyperalgesia); lidocaine 1–1.5 mg/kg/h (caution > 24 h), methadone 0.1–0.2 mg/kg IV at induction (long-acting opioid)
REGIONAL: ESP (erector spinae plane) block bilateral T10–L1 single-shot or catheter — reduces opioid; surgeon-administered wound infiltration; intrathecal morphine 100–500 mcg (selected cases)
POST-OP: opioid PCA + paracetamol + NSAID (if not contraindicated post-op) + gabapentinoid; multimodal documentation
═══ PAEDIATRIC / SCOLIOSIS-SPECIFIC ═══
Restrictive lung disease in scoliosis (Cobb > 70°) — pre-op PFTs essential; postop respiratory failure risk
Cardiac involvement (Cobb > 100°, neuromuscular scoliosis with DMD/SMA): pre-op echo + cardiology review
Cerebral palsy + neuromuscular scoliosis: malignant hyperthermia risk if implicated muscular dystrophy → trigger-free anaesthesia (TIVA + no volatile + no sux)
Higher TXA dose 30 mg/kg + 10 mg/kg/h (more bleeding per BSA)
Higher transfusion (cell salvage + group-specific blood)
Magnesium 30 mg/kg for muscle relaxant (titrate to TOF if NMB allowed)
Ketamine + dexmedetomidine adjuncts for prolonged opioid-sparing; PCA + adjuncts post-op
Wake-up test rare now (MEP standard) but ensure team capability if signals lost
═══ POST-OP ===
ICU/HDU for complex cases; ward fast-track for single-level uncomplicated

Watch for: bleeding (drain output), spinal haematoma (urgent MRI if new neuro deficit — surgical emergency, decompress within hours), respiratory failure (scoliosis), pulmonary embolism (long surgery + prone)
Early mobilisation per ERAS spine (day 1)
Pain assessment + opioid weaning + transitioning to oral analgesia

considerations: ═══ ASSESSMENT BEFORE EVERY CASE ═══
TBSA reassessment: Lund-Browder chart (NOT Wallace rule of nines — head proportion changes with age: infant head ≈ 18 % vs adult 9 %)
Burn depth: superficial / partial-thickness / full-thickness; deep burns = no nerve fibres = LESS pain at burn site but DONOR site is painful
Inhalational injury history: closed-space fire, soot in nares, hoarseness, stridor, COHb

Phase of burn: ACUTE (< 48 h — hypovolaemic shock, fluid resus) vs HYPERMETABOLIC (> 48 h — high CO, high O₂ demand, tachycardia, hyperthermia 38–38.5 °C is physiological) vs LATE (> 2 weeks — repeated dressings/grafts, contractures, scarring)
═══ AIRWAY ═══
Facial/neck burns + repeated procedures → potential difficult airway (contracture, microstomia, scar tissue)
Inhalation injury → airway oedema progressive over 24–48 h; INTUBATE EARLY if any doubt (stridor, hoarseness, soot, singed nasal hair, closed-space exposure) BEFORE swelling closes airway

Cuffed ETT preferred (allows ventilation despite chest/neck oedema); secure with cloth tape circumferentially around head (adhesive tape will not stick to burned skin); document position carefully — accidental extubation = catastrophic in oedematous airway
Awake fibreoptic / video laryngoscopy if anticipated difficult; ENT/burn surgeon on standby for emergency surgical airway in severe cases
═══ VASCULAR ACCESS ═══

Often difficult — burned + previously cannulated extremities; consider intraosseous early in shock; central access (femoral often preferred — less burned); peripheral large-bore through burned skin acceptable if needed
═══ FLUIDS — MODIFIED PARKLAND FORMULA (paeds, per ABA 2024) ═══
Resuscitation phase (first 24 h, > 10 % TBSA): Lactated Ringer 3–4 mL/kg × % TBSA — HALF in first 8 h (from TIME OF INJURY), HALF in next 16 h
PLUS maintenance fluid (paediatric — added because of higher BSA/volume ratio):
• 4 mL/kg/h for first 10 kg
• PLUS 2 mL/kg/h for 10–20 kg
• PLUS 1 mL/kg/h for each kg > 20 kg
• Use D5 ½ NS or D5 LR for maintenance (children < 30 kg need glucose — limited glycogen stores)
INHALATION INJURY: increase fluids by 30–50 %
ELECTRICAL BURNS: up to 9 mL/kg/% TBSA; target UO 1.5–2 mL/kg/h (myoglobinuria)
Target UO: 1–2 mL/kg/h (paediatric — higher than adult 0.5–1)
Albumin 5 %: typically introduced after first 24 h (or earlier in severe — controversial); maintain albumin > 20 g/L
═══ TEMPERATURE — CRITICAL ═══
Burns lose massive heat (no skin barrier); operating room WARM (32 °C ambient, 70–80 % humidity per WFSA), forced-air warmer, warmed IV fluids, fluid warmer, warmed irrigation, head cover
Target core ≥ 36.5 °C; hypothermia → coagulopathy + arrhythmia + delayed wound healing
═══ ANAESTHESIA AGENTS ═══
KETAMINE = ideal for paediatric burns (analgesia + amnesia + bronchodilation + haemodynamic stability + preserved airway reflexes): induction 1–2 mg/kg IV or 4–6 mg/kg IM; infusion 1–3 mg/kg/h
Avoid suxamethonium FROM 24 h to 18 MONTHS POST-BURN (up-regulated extrajunctional AChR → potentially fatal hyperkalaemia; risk persists until full epithelialisation)
Use rocuronium 0.6–1.2 mg/kg (sugammadex reversal if Mg²⁺ not low); cisatracurium acceptable
Non-depolarising NMB RESISTANCE develops > 1 week post-burn → may need 2–3× normal dose; monitor with TOF
Hypermetabolic state → increased anaesthetic requirement; titrate to BIS if available
═══ ANALGESIA — HIGH REQUIREMENT, TOLERANCE ═══

Multimodal: paracetamol 15 mg/kg, opioid (morphine 0.1 mg/kg IV titrated, fentanyl 1–2 mcg/kg, remifentanil infusion for procedures), ketamine adjunct, dexmedetomidine 0.5–1 mcg/kg/h, regional blocks where feasible (e.g. fascia iliaca for thigh donor sites)
NSAIDs caution if AKI risk (rhabdomyolysis from deep burns)

═══ POST-OP ═══
Watch for compartment syndrome (deep burns) — escharotomy/fasciotomy if needed
Hypermetabolic state: increased nutrition requirements (1.5–2× basal); enteral feeding asap
Repeated procedures = psychological trauma → child life specialist, anxiety reduction, parent presence at induction

COHb if recent (< 24 h): displays normal SpO₂ but actually hypoxic — ABG with co-oximetry; 100 % O₂ until COHb < 5 % (half-life 4–6 h on room air, 60–90 min on 100 % O₂, 20–30 min hyperbaric)
═══ NMB & DRUG CONSIDERATIONS ═══

**AVOID SUXAMETHONIUM** from 24 h post-burn to 18 MONTHS post-burn (or full epithelialisation) — up-regulated extrajunctional acetylcholine receptors → MASSIVE K⁺ release (rise of 4–10 mEq/L) → cardiac arrest. This is a hard rule per ABA/BJA Educ 2022
**NMB resistance** develops > 1 week post-burn (extrajunctional AChR up-regulation also reduces non-depolariser potency): may need 2–3× normal rocuronium dose; quantitative TOF monitoring essential
**Opioid tolerance** in late phase from chronic exposure → 2–5× higher requirements; rotate opioids, add ketamine + dexmedetomidine to reduce escalation
Drug PK altered: hypermetabolic state → faster clearance of hepatically cleared drugs (propofol, fentanyl); larger Vd for hydrophilic drugs (acute phase oedema) → may need loading dose
═══ FLUID & BLEEDING ═══
Excision blood loss: ~ 0.5–1 mL/cm² superficial tangential, up to 2–4 mL/cm² deep excision; large grafts → litres of loss
Pre-incision tumescent infiltration (LA + adrenaline 1:1,000,000) reduces blood loss substantially — coordinate with surgeon
TXA 1 g IV pre-incision considered for large excisions (off-label but supported by 2023–24 evidence)
Group & cross-match — 2–4 PRBC for major debridement; activate MTP for > 30 % TBSA debridement
Goal-directed fluid (stroke volume variation): avoid over-resuscitation (worsens oedema + ARDS)
═══ TEMPERATURE ═══
Burns lose massive heat (no skin barrier); operating room WARM (28–32 °C), forced-air warmer, warmed IV fluids, warmed irrigation; target core ≥ 36.5 °C
Hypothermia → coagulopathy + arrhythmia + delayed wound healing + infection
═══ ANALGESIA — MULTIMODAL HIGH-DOSE ═══
Ketamine 0.15–0.5 mg/kg/h IV infusion (anti-hyperalgesic + opioid-sparing + reduces chronic pain)
Paracetamol 1 g IV q6h (max 4 g/day)
Opioid PCA post-op (often 2–3× standard doses); methadone consideration for refractory tolerance
Dexmedetomidine 0.2–1 mcg/kg/h infusion (anxiolysis + opioid-sparing; mind hypotension)
Regional where feasible: fascia iliaca for thigh donor sites, brachial plexus for upper limb work
Lidocaine infusion 1–2 mg/kg/h (caution if hepatic injury or > 24 h continuous use)
═══ POST-OP ═══
Extubation: assess cuff leak before extubation if previously intubated for inhalation (re-intubation difficult if airway oedema persists)
ICU/HDU if extensive debridement, ongoing fluid shifts, sepsis risk
Watch for: rhabdomyolysis (deep electrical burns), compartment syndrome, sepsis (commonest cause of late mortality)

anaesthesia.preferred: GA + RSI + arterial line + 2× large-bore IV (or IO) + early MTP activation + DCR principles (per EAST 2017 + Schmulevich Transfusion 2024)
considerations: ═══ DAMAGE CONTROL RESUSCITATION (DCR) — 5 PILLARS ═══
1. PERMISSIVE HYPOTENSION (until bleeding controlled): SBP 80–90 (MAP ~ 50–65) in blunt/penetrating trauma WITHOUT TBI; normal pressure with TBI (avoid secondary brain injury — MAP ≥ 80, SBP ≥ 110)

2. HAEMOSTATIC RESUSCITATION: balanced product ratio 1:1:1 (PRBC:FFP:platelets) as INITIAL approach; transition to TEG/ROTEM-guided once available (EAST conditional recommendation 2017 — TEG-guided DCR has mortality benefit per Gonzalez 2016 RCT)

3. AVOID CRYSTALLOID OVERLOAD: max 1–2 L LR/Plasmalyte before blood (older "3:1 rule" abandoned — dilutes coagulation factors, worsens acidosis); after that → blood products only until bleeding controlled

4. EARLY HAEMORRHAGE CONTROL: surgical (damage control surgery), tourniquet (extremity), pelvic binder, REBOA (zone 1 supraceliac for non-compressible torso haemorrhage if available — see id="damage-control")
5. PREVENT THE LETHAL TRIAD: hypothermia + acidosis + coagulopathy reinforce each other — aggressive correction
═══ MASSIVE TRANSFUSION PROTOCOL (MTP) — ACTIVATE EARLY ═══
ABC score ≥ 2 OR shock index > 1.0 OR ongoing transfusion need = trigger MTP
Components per cooler: 6 PRBC + 6 FFP + 1 apheresis platelets (≈ 1:1:1)
Cryoprecipitate: 10 units when fibrinogen < 1.5 g/L (< 2.0 g/L in obstetric trauma)
WHOLE BLOOD (if available): increasing evidence base; 1 U whole blood = 1 PRBC + 1 FFP + small platelet equivalent
Calcium: maintain ionised Ca²⁺ > 1.0 mmol/L (1 g CaCl₂ after every 4 U PRBC empirically — citrate toxicity)
═══ TRANEXAMIC ACID (CRASH-2 / CRASH-3) ═══
TXA 1 g IV bolus over 10 min + 1 g infusion over 8 h, within 3 h of injury (CRASH-2 — mortality reduction 1.5 %; greatest benefit < 1 h)
TBI with GCS 9–12 (CRASH-3): TXA 1 g + 1 g/8 h, within 3 h — reduces head-injury-related deaths
Combat/austere alternative: single 2 g IV push (per JTS DCR guideline 2018; PATCH-Trauma 2023 found no benefit BUT no harm)
AVOID > 3 h post-injury (CRASH-2 showed harm with later administration)
═══ AIRWAY MANAGEMENT ═══
RSI standard (full stomach + possible head injury): ketamine 1–2 mg/kg (haemodynamic stability in shock) + rocuronium 1.2 mg/kg (faster onset, longer duration than sux for stable airway)
Avoid suxamethonium if: > 24 h post-burn (NOT relevant in acute trauma), pre-existing neuromuscular disease, hyperkalaemia
Cervical spine immobilisation (manual in-line stabilisation, hard collar) — video laryngoscopy preferred (less neck movement than direct)
Anticipate difficult airway: maxillofacial trauma, neck haematoma, airway burn, blood/secretions
═══ TEMPERATURE — CRITICAL ═══
Active warming from minute 1: forced-air warmer, warmed IV fluids (38–40 °C in fluid warmer / rapid infuser), warmed irrigation, theatre to 24 °C minimum, blankets over non-surgical areas
Target ≥ 36 °C; trauma hypothermia (< 35) doubles mortality
═══ AGE-SPECIFIC ═══
PAEDIATRIC POLYTRAUMA:
• Weight-based MTP: 10 mL/kg PRBC + 10 mL/kg FFP + 10 mL/kg platelets
• TXA: 15 mg/kg (max 1 g) bolus + 2 mg/kg/h infusion for 8 h
• Permissive hypotension UNPROVEN in paeds — maintain MAP age-appropriate (5th centile)
• Higher body surface area / volume → hypothermia faster
• C-spine: occipital pad NOT needed in younger child (large occiput already produces flexion); use trauma backboard with cutout or built-up torso
• IO access threshold low — 90 s rule
ELDERLY POLYTRAUMA:
• Lower haemodynamic reserve — beta-blocker mask tachycardia; small drop in haemoglobin poorly tolerated
• Anticoagulant reversal urgent (warfarin → 4F-PCC + vit K; DOAC → andexanet alfa / idarucizumab; anti-platelet → consider platelet transfusion + DDAVP)
• Frailty score predicts outcome better than ISS
• Lower threshold for occult injury — falls from standing height can cause major intracranial bleeds in atrophy
═══ HEAD INJURY (CO-EXISTING) ═══
If TBI co-exists: target MAP ≥ 80 (NOT permissive hypotension); avoid hypoxia (SpO₂ < 90), hypercapnia, hyperglycaemia
Mannitol 0.25–1 g/kg or HTS 3 % 3–5 mL/kg if signs of raised ICP (see craniotomy-trauma entry)
Levetiracetam 20–60 mg/kg load (adult) / 60 mg/kg (paeds) for early seizure prophylaxis × 7 days per BTF
CRASH-3 dose of TXA as above
═══ MONITORING ═══
Continuous: ECG, SpO₂, BP (arterial preferred), EtCO₂, temp, UO
Serial: lactate (q30–60 min — clearance > 50 % at 24 h = good prognosis), ABG, ROTEM/TEG, ionised Ca²⁺, glucose, K⁺
Base deficit > 6 = ongoing shock; lactate > 4 = serious tissue hypoperfusion
═══ DAMAGE CONTROL SURGERY (DCS) ═══
Indications: hypothermia < 34 °C, pH < 7.2, base deficit > 15, coagulopathy (INR > 1.5 or TEG abnormal), ongoing transfusion need

Abbreviated surgery: control bleeding (pack, clamp, shunt), control contamination (resect, no anastomosis); leave abdomen OPEN (temporary closure — Bogota bag, VAC); return to ICU for re-warming + correction; back to OR in 24–48 h for definitive surgery
See id="damage-control" for surgical specifics
═══ POST-OP ═══

ICU intubated; ongoing resuscitation; tertiary survey within 24 h (40 % miss rate of secondary injuries); multimodal analgesia (avoid epidural if coagulopathic); DVT prophylaxis once bleeding stopped (24 h); early enteral nutrition

anaesthesia.preferred: GA + arterial line PRE-induction (radial) + 9F introducer for PAC + CVC + TEE (mandatory) + cell salvage + MTP activated
considerations: ═══ PATIENT POPULATION ═══
INTERMACS classification (1–7): I (critical cardiogenic shock — emergency), II (progressive decline on inotropes), III (stable on inotropes), IV (resting symptoms), V–VII (less severe)
Indication: bridge to transplant (BTT), destination therapy (DT), bridge to recovery (BTR), bridge to candidacy (BTC)
Most are INTERMACS 2–4 — on chronic inotropes, EF often < 20 %, secondary pulmonary HTN, cardiorenal syndrome, cardiac cachexia
Common devices: HeartMate 3 (current standard), HeartWare HVAD (largely withdrawn 2021), older HeartMate II
═══ PRE-OP OPTIMISATION ═══
Echocardiogram + right heart cath: PVR, TAPSE, RVEF, RA pressure, PA pressure, CVP, PCWP — KEY data for RV failure prediction
EUROMACS-RHF score / CRITT score for RV failure risk stratification (RA > 10, RV/LV ratio > 0.75, TAPSE < 14 mm, severe TR = high risk)
RV failure risk factors: female, BMI < 23, ICU pre-op, INR > 1.2, BUN > 39, mechanical ventilation, severe TR
OPTIMISE PRE-OP: diuresis to euvolaemia (NOT dry — RV preload needed), inotrope optimisation, treat pulmonary HTN (sildenafil, iNO trial), anticoagulation management
Cross-match 4–6 PRBC + FFP + platelets; cell salvage set up; MTP ready
═══ INDUCTION — FAILING HEART ═══
Arterial line + adequate vasopressor support BEFORE induction
AVOID: drops in preload (large IV bolus contraindicated — already overloaded), contractility (high-dose propofol), and SVR (rapid sympatholysis)
Etomidate 0.2–0.3 mg/kg + fentanyl 5–10 mcg/kg + slow titration; AVOID large propofol bolus
Ketamine 0.5–1 mg/kg acceptable (preserves SVR + contractility) — but mind PVR rise (concern overstated in modern data)
Rocuronium 1.2 mg/kg (or vecuronium); avoid sux if hyperkalaemia / chronic illness
Continue inotrope infusions (milrinone / dobutamine / dopamine) through induction
═══ PRE-CPB ═══
Heparin 300–400 U/kg (ACT > 480 s) — but mind pre-existing coagulopathy + anticoagulant exposure (warfarin → 4F-PCC reversal if INR > 2.0 day of surgery)
Anti-fibrinolytic: TXA 30 mg/kg load + 16 mg/kg/h (Bentall-style dosing for long case + bleeding risk)
Avoid air embolism (closed-system PIVs, vent IV bags) — concern for AV ECMO + neuro
═══ CPB AND IMPLANT ═══
Standard CPB conduct (see CPB weaning checklist for adult)
INFLOW cannula in LV apex; OUTFLOW graft to ascending aorta
De-airing CRITICAL (LV + outflow graft) — TEE multi-view; right Trendelenburg; CO₂ field flooding; aspirate via outflow vent before LVAD start
═══ LVAD INITIATION ═══
GRADUAL SPEED INCREASE — start low flow (3–4 L/min), increase over 5–10 min to target (5–6 L/min for HM3)
TEE-guided RV assessment continuously during speed-up — septal position (midline = optimal; bulging into LV = under-speed; bulging into RV = over-speed → "septal shift" + RV dysfunction)
OVER-SPEEDING is the commonest cause of post-LVAD RV failure: rapid LV unloading → septal shift LEFTWARD → RV geometry distorted → RV failure
Avoid: under-filling LV ("suction event" — septum collides with inflow cannula, ventricular arrhythmia, low flow alarms)
═══ RV FAILURE PREVENTION (PRIMARY GOAL) ═══
Pulmonary vasodilator FROM START of weaning: iNO 20–40 ppm OR nebulised epoprostenol 50 ng/kg/min
Milrinone 0.375–0.75 mcg/kg/min (continuous from pre-induction often)
Adrenaline 0.05–0.15 mcg/kg/min as primary inotrope
Avoid systemic vasoconstrictors that raise PVR (high-dose noradrenaline) — use vasopressin 0.04 U/min for SVR if needed (minimal PVR effect)
TARGETS: CVP < 15, MAP 70–90, PVR < 3 Wood units, low LAP (< 15)
═══ RV FAILURE TREATMENT (IF OCCURS) ═══
Continuous TEE monitoring; if RV dilation + hypokinesis + rising CVP + falling MAP DESPITE optimised inotropes/vasodilators:
STEP 1: Reduce LVAD speed (less LV unloading, septum re-centres) + maximise inotropes + maximise iNO
STEP 2: Insert temporary RVAD — percutaneous Impella RP via femoral vein, or central CentriMag via PA + RA cannulation (per Rodenas-Alesina 2022 review)
STEP 3: VA-ECMO if RVAD insufficient (worse outcomes)
═══ POST-CPB / WEANING ═══
Slow protamine (NEVER bolus) — 1 mg per 100 U residual heparin; vasopressor primed; TEE on RV view
Bleeding management: ROTEM-guided (fibrinogen if FIBTEM A10 < 10, PCC if EXTEM CT prolonged after protamine, platelets if < 100 — higher threshold than usual CPB)
Cell salvage continued
═══ POST-OP ═══
CICU intubated 12–48 h; sedation continued until extubation criteria met
Anticoagulation: bivalirudin OR heparin transition to warfarin (target INR 2.0–3.0); aspirin 81–100 mg added
CVP < 15 maintained for RV preload; avoid volume overload

Watch for: bleeding, RV failure (early or late), GI bleeding (AV malformations — Heyde syndrome), stroke (thrombo-embolic vs haemorrhagic on anticoagulation), driveline infection, pump thrombosis (HM3 lowest rate)
Ultra-fast-track extubation possible in selected stable patients (INTERMACS 3–4) per propensity-matched cohort study — reduces pneumonia, delirium, RVF, ICU stay

considerations: ═══ CRAWFORD CLASSIFICATION (DETERMINES STRATEGY) ═══
Crawford I: distal to LSCA → above renal arteries (most spinal cord risk — Adamkiewicz often included)
Crawford II: distal to LSCA → aortic bifurcation (HIGHEST risk: SCI 6–11 %, mortality 7–15 %)
Crawford III: distal descending thoracic → bifurcation
Crawford IV: upper abdominal aorta → bifurcation
Crawford V: distal descending → above renal
Extent II = highest risk for paraplegia + visceral ischaemia + AKI
═══ PATIENT POPULATION ═══
Often: connective tissue disease (Marfan, Loeys-Dietz, vascular EDS), chronic dissection, atherosclerotic aneurysm, post-traumatic, infective; many elderly with COPD, CKD, CAD, prior cardiac surgery
Symptomatic (back/chest pain, hoarseness, dysphagia) → urgent; ruptured → emergency surgery — much worse outcomes
═══ PRE-OP ASSESSMENT ═══
CT angio mapping: extent, dissection, intercostal/Adamkiewicz origin (often T9–T12 left side), visceral patency, branch vessel involvement
Echo + LV function + valvular assessment; cardiac cath if CAD; carotid Doppler (cerebral protection planning)
PFTs essential (left thoracotomy + OLV); chronic smokers / COPD baseline
Renal function baseline (high AKI risk); urinalysis; consider HD planning if baseline CKD
Connective tissue workup if young / Marfan features
Cross-match 8–10 PRBC + FFP + platelets + cryo; cell salvage; MTP activated
═══ CSF DRAIN PLACEMENT (CLASS I, EACTS/STS 2024) ═══
Mandatory for open TAAA repair (especially extents I–III); CSF drain placed pre-induction or post-induction (sterile technique, lumbar approach L3-L4 or L4-L5)
Target ICP/CSFP: maintain < 10 mmHg intraop + 48–72 h post-op
Drainage strategy: INTERMITTENT preferred over continuous (reduces subarachnoid haemorrhage risk per Cochrane); drain when CSFP > 10 mmHg, max 10–15 mL/h, target SCPP > 60 mmHg
Watch for: subdural/epidural haematoma (severe headache, focal deficit), CSF leak, infection
═══ MONITORING — COMPREHENSIVE ═══
Bilateral arterial lines: RIGHT RADIAL (cerebral perfusion proximal to clamp) + FEMORAL (distal perfusion below clamp, also for endo cannula access)
NIRS bilateral (cerebral + somatic — limb perfusion); TEE for cardiac function + dissection assessment
MEP + SSEP: continuous through cross-clamp + reperfusion (per Coselli 2023 — MEP more sensitive, SSEP more specific)
MEP loss INTERPRETATION: early reversible SCI sign — IMMEDIATE response algorithm:
1. Reattach intercostal arteries T8–T12 (collateral network)
2. Re-establish pulsatile flow to pelvis (distal aortic perfusion ON)
3. Increase MAP > 90 (target SCPP > 80)
4. Drain CSF to ICP < 10
5. Optimise Hb > 10
6. Increase distal perfusion pressure > 80
SSEP loss = advanced ischaemia (reaching irreversible) — urgent reattachment
CORE TEMP monitor + bladder temp + tympanic
═══ AIRWAY / VENTILATION ===
Left double-lumen tube (right-sided risk of RUL obstruction); fibreoptic bronchoscopy confirmation
OLV (right lung up) for left thoracotomy: lung-protective (TV 4–6 mL/kg PBW, PEEP 5, plateau < 25); CPAP to non-ventilated lung if hypoxia
After repair: switch to two-lung ventilation; expect oedema in collapsed lung (re-expansion oedema, lung protective ventilation continued)
═══ SPINAL CORD PROTECTION — MULTI-MODAL (EACTS/STS 2024) ===
A. CSF drainage to ICP < 10 mmHg (above)
B. Distal aortic perfusion (left heart bypass — LA → femoral artery — for Crawford I/II/III): maintains perfusion below clamp, reduces SCI from 15 % → 5 %
C. Selective intercostal artery REATTACHMENT (T8–T12 critically; Adamkiewicz region T9–T11 left side)
D. MODERATE HYPOTHERMIA: systemic 32–34 °C (cools cord metabolism); regional spinal cord cooling (epidural cold perfusion 10–12 °C) at some centres

E. Pharmacological adjuncts (lower evidence): naloxone trial (0.001 mg/kg/h reduces SCI in some series), barbiturate (thiopentone 1–3 mg/kg as cold cardioplegia adjunct); intrathecal papaverine investigational
F. Avoid hyperthermia (worsens SCI), hyperglycaemia (controversial — keep BG < 180), hypocarbia (vasoconstricts cord)
═══ CEREBRAL PROTECTION (PROXIMAL ARCH WORK) ===
For aortic arch involvement: DHCA 18–22 °C + antegrade cerebral perfusion (ACP — right axillary cannula 10 mL/kg/min, target NIRS preservation) OR retrograde cerebral perfusion (RCP via SVC)
Cooling: cool slowly (3 °C/min max), avoid > 6 °C gradient; thiopentone 5–10 mg/kg pre-arrest (some centres) — burst suppression on EEG
NIRS bilateral monitors ACP adequacy; if asymmetric → check cannula position / left vertebral retrograde flow
═══ VISCERAL + RENAL PROTECTION ===
Selective visceral perfusion (cold blood / crystalloid) during cross-clamp at celiac/SMA/renal
Cold renal perfusion: cold Hartmann's 100–200 mL each kidney (renal hypothermia), mannitol 0.25–0.5 g/kg pre-clamp
Maintain MAP > 65, UO > 0.5 mL/kg/h; furosemide PRN; AKI bundle (avoid nephrotoxins, normovolaemia)
═══ HAEMODYNAMIC MANAGEMENT ===
PRE-CLAMP: smooth induction, anti-fibrinolytic (TXA 30 mg/kg + 16 mg/kg/h), opioid + vasopressor primed

CROSS-CLAMP APPLICATION: SUDDEN ↑ SVR + ↑ afterload + ↑ LV wall stress — pre-treat with vasodilator (nitroprusside / nicardipine / clevidipine), beta-blocker (esmolol), titrated; avoid hypertensive crisis
CROSS-CLAMP RELEASE (UNCLAMPING): SUDDEN ↓ SVR + acid + K⁺ + vasoactive mediators flooding circulation → HYPOTENSION ("unclamping shock")
• Slow unclamp (collaboration with surgeon) over 1–2 min
• Volume loaded pre-unclamp (CVP 12–15)
• Vasopressor ready: noradrenaline + adrenaline boluses + CaCl₂ + NaHCO₃ if acid + insulin/glucose if K⁺ high
• Resume aggressive warming after distal perfusion
═══ BLEEDING MANAGEMENT ===

Massive transfusion expected (12–20 + units); ROTEM-guided: fibrinogen if FIBTEM A10 < 10, PCC if EXTEM CT prolonged, platelets if < 100 (higher threshold than other cardiac), cryoprecipitate for fibrinogen < 2 g/L
Cell salvage continuous; minimise crystalloid (dilutional coagulopathy)
Heparin per protocol (lower than CPB for left heart bypass; full heparinisation 300–400 U/kg for full CPB/DHCA)
═══ POST-OP ===
ICU intubated 24–48 h; CSF drain continued 48–72 h, target ICP < 10; MAP > 80–100 (SCPP > 60); Hb > 10
Neurological exam q1h (lower limb strength, sensation) — delayed paraplegia can occur day 1–3 even with intact intraop MEP/SSEP — emergency response: increase MAP > 100, drain CSF, exclude haematoma

CSF drain removal: gradual; clamp trial 6–12 h, monitor for new deficit; remove with sterile technique; document; some keep longer if deficit detected

considerations: ═══ INDICATIONS ═══
COPD/emphysema, IPF/pulmonary fibrosis, cystic fibrosis (often bilateral), pulmonary hypertension (idiopathic / CTEPH), bronchiectasis, alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, sarcoidosis
PAEDIATRIC indications: cystic fibrosis (commonest), idiopathic PHT, surfactant deficiency, post-Fontan failure
Single (SLT) vs bilateral (BLT): BLT preferred for septic lung disease (CF, bronchiectasis); SLT acceptable for COPD/IPF in older recipients
═══ PRE-OP ASSESSMENT ═══
Lung allocation score (LAS) for urgency; PFTs (FEV1, FVC, DLCO); 6MWT; echocardiogram (mean PAP, RV function, LV function); right heart cath (PVR — separates idiopathic PHT from secondary)
Anticipate difficult IV access (chronically ill, prior central lines), difficult intubation if facial features changed by chronic steroids
Frailty + sarcopenia common — opioid-sensitive, NMB resistance to plasma cholinesterase substrates
═══ INDUCTION ═══
Pre-oxygenate at sitting position (often orthopnoeic); avoid lying flat until induction
Bilateral arterial lines (right radial + femoral — ECMO arterial cannula may compromise one); peripheral large-bore (16G × 2); CVC + 9F introducer for PAC + rapid infusion
Induction agents tolerated: etomidate 0.3 mg/kg + fentanyl 5–10 mcg/kg ± low-dose ketamine; AVOID large propofol bolus (vasodilation)
Rocuronium 1.2 mg/kg or vecuronium 0.1 mg/kg (sux contraindicated if elevated K⁺ or rhabdomyolysis history)
DLT placement confirmed by fibreoptic bronchoscopy; bilateral chest auscultation; capnography
PHT patients VULNERABLE to induction — RV failure can occur from PEEP, hypoxia, hypercarbia, vasodilator-induced SVR drop; have iNO + adrenaline immediately ready
═══ POSITIONING ═══
Supine for clamshell (bilateral); lateral for single-lung; both for SLT-via-sternotomy
Clamshell incision (transverse sternotomy) is more painful but gives best access for bilateral
═══ INTRAOPERATIVE ECMO (NOW STANDARD AT MAJOR CENTRES) ═══
Central VA-ECMO (right atrium + ascending aorta) or peripheral VA-ECMO (femoral or via existing arterial access) — preferred over CPB per 2024 evidence:
• Better controlled reperfusion of graft → less PGD
• Less inflammatory response than CPB (no cardiotomy reservoir, smaller priming volume)
• Allows protective ventilation throughout
• Heparin requirement lower (ACT 180–220 vs > 480 on CPB)
• Per Wuxi 2025: central VA-ECMO had less PGD3 at 72 h vs peripheral; choice per centre + patient
CPB reserved for: planned cardiac intervention, intracardiac shunt repair, persistent haemodynamic failure on ECMO
═══ ONE-LUNG VENTILATION (PRE-IMPLANT) ═══
Lung-protective settings: TV 4–6 mL/kg PBW, plateau < 25 cmH₂O, PEEP 5, driving pressure < 14, permissive hypercapnia if needed
FiO₂ titrated to SpO₂ 92–95 % (avoid hyperoxia + reactive oxygen damage to graft)
If hypoxia despite optimisation → initiate ECMO (low threshold)
═══ IMPLANTATION (PER LUNG, BILATERAL = SEQUENTIAL) ═══
Recipient pneumonectomy; donor lung anastomosis (bronchus → PA → PV/LA); BEFORE reperfusion: flush graft with cold preservation solution
═══ REPERFUSION — SLOW + CONTROLLED ═══
"Slow ECMO wean" with controlled reperfusion = MAINSTAY of PGD prevention per Medical University of Vienna protocol
Goal: gradually transfer pulmonary blood flow to new lung over 5–10 min (NOT sudden full flow → reperfusion injury, oedema, ARDS)
Restrictive fluid: keep "dry lung" — accept lower CVP (5–8), use vasopressors before fluid; goal-directed (SVV)
Pulmonary vasodilator: iNO 20–40 ppm from reperfusion (RV protection + improves V/Q)
Lung-protective ventilation continues throughout (low Vt, PEEP 5–8); reduce FiO₂ to keep SpO₂ 92–95 %
═══ PRIMARY GRAFT DYSFUNCTION (PGD) — MAJOR THREAT ═══
ISHLT 2017 definition: PaO₂/FiO₂ ratio + radiographic infiltrates at 24/48/72 h post-transplant
PGD-3 (severe, P/F < 200 + infiltrates) at 72 h = highest mortality, most common cause of early death
Risk factors: prolonged ischaemic time, donor smoking, recipient PHT, large transfusion, oversize mismatch

TREATMENT: maintain ECMO post-op (VV-ECMO preferred per Pittsburgh 2024 — lower airway anastomosis complications than VA-ECMO); prone positioning; lung-protective ventilation; restrictive fluid; treat infection
═══ POST-CPB / POST-ECMO WEANING ═══
Continue iNO; titrate ECMO flow down gradually; chest closed only when haemodynamically stable + lung volume optimised
Immunosuppression: methylprednisolone 500–1000 mg at reperfusion (or smaller doses to avoid airway healing impairment); basiliximab; tacrolimus + MMF post-op
═══ ANALGESIA ═══

Thoracic epidural traditionally favoured (clamshell incision is painful) — BUT if planned ECMO + anticoagulation, epidural can be deferred to post-op or replaced with bilateral paravertebral / serratus anterior plane / ESP blocks

═══ POST-OP ═══

Watch for: PGD (24–72 h), bronchial anastomosis dehiscence, airway anastomosis ischaemia (VV-ECMO protective vs VA), rejection (1–2 weeks), CMV reactivation (later), opportunistic infection

═══ PAEDIATRIC-SPECIFIC ═══

considerations: ═══ AETIOLOGY & POPULATION ═══

Most common indications: biliary atresia (post-Kasai), metabolic disease (urea cycle defects, tyrosinaemia, Wilson's, OTC deficiency), acute liver failure (paracetamol, hepatitis, idiopathic), HCC in chronic disease
Graft types: whole organ (deceased donor), reduced-size (segments 2-3, left lateral segment), split-liver (one donor → 2 recipients), living donor (parent → child)
Size discordance: large-for-recipient graft → more pronounced post-reperfusion hypotension (filling of large vessel volume); abdominal compartment syndrome risk if oversized → delayed closure
═══ PRE-OP ═══
No premedication unless severe anxiety (encephalopathy risk in fulminant failure); parents in induction room if young child + stable
Coagulopathy + thrombocytopenia: avoid IM, neuraxial; cross-match 2–4 PRBC + FFP + platelets + cryo
Hyponatraemia (often Na⁺ 125–130 in chronic liver failure): correct slowly pre-op; rapid correction → osmotic demyelination
Glucose: maintain via dextrose-containing maintenance (2.5–5 % dextrose in balanced solution); risk of hypoglycaemia (poor glycogen stores) and hyperglycaemia (stress)
Previous Kasai → extensive adhesions, vascular distortion, bleeding during dissection
Hepatopulmonary syndrome (HPS): orthodeoxia (SpO₂ drops with sitting), intrapulmonary shunts → resolves post-transplant
═══ INTRAOPERATIVE PHASES (same 4 as adult — see main liver-transplant entry) ═══
PRE-ANHEPATIC: dissection bleeding; vasopressor support (noradrenaline 0.05–0.5 mcg/kg/min, vasopressin 0.0003–0.001 U/kg/min); ROTEM-guided products; low CVP strategy if possible

ANHEPATIC: CO drops ~ 50 % from caval clamp; piggyback technique preferred in paeds (preserves IVC flow); avoid hepatic-cleared drugs (use remi, cisatracurium, propofol TCI); methylprednisolone 10 mg/kg IV (max 1 g) before unclamping
PRE-REPERFUSION CHECKLIST (5 min pre-unclamp):
• K⁺ < 4.0 mEq/L (per Çekmen 2024 paeds review — paeds less tolerant of swings)
• Ionised Ca²⁺ > 1.0 mmol/L (consider continuous CaCl₂ infusion 5–10 mg/kg/h — immature citrate clearance)
• Core temp ≥ 35.5 °C
• Vasopressors primed + adrenaline + atropine drawn up
REPERFUSION: PRS in 20–40 % paediatric LT; same triad (cold + acidotic + hyperkalaemic blood); IMMEDIATE:
• Adrenaline 1 mcg/kg IV bolus (max 100 mcg) titrated
• CaCl₂ 10–20 mg/kg (max 1 g)
• Atropine 20 mcg/kg (bradycardia, min 100 mcg, max 600 mcg)
• Hyperkalaemia (K⁺ > 6): insulin 0.1 U/kg + glucose 0.5 g/kg, NaHCO₃ 1 mmol/kg, salbutamol nebuliser
• Refractory vasoplegia: methylene blue 1 mg/kg over 10 min
NEOHEPATIC: glucose extreme lability — q15 min monitoring; albumin 5–20 % for volume; avoid Hartmann's (lactate load); HAT/PVT high risk in paeds — low-dose heparin/aspirin per centre
═══ POST-OP ═══
PICU intubated 24–48 h typically (longer if reduced-size graft + abdominal tightness)
Delayed sternal/abdominal closure considered if large-for-recipient graft + venous congestion
Doppler q12h × 72 h for HAT/PVT (paeds have higher rates)
Immunosuppression: methylpred taper + tacrolimus + basiliximab (per centre); MMF + steroid taper later
Hypertension common post-op (calcineurin inhibitor + steroid) → may need clonidine/amlodipine

═══ PRE-OP ASSESSMENT ===

═══ AIRWAY ===

═══ FLUID + TEMPERATURE ===

═══ ANALGESIA — ERAS PAEDS SPINE ===

INTRAOP: methadone 0.1 mg/kg IV at induction (long-acting opioid base); ketamine 0.15–0.5 mg/kg/h infusion; dexmedetomidine 0.3–0.7 mcg/kg/h
REGIONAL: bilateral ESP catheters T8–T10 (now standard at major paediatric centres — reduces opioid 50 %, faster mobilisation); intrathecal morphine 5 mcg/kg (max 250 mcg) by surgeon at end of case

═══ POST-OP ===

Watch for: respiratory failure (especially NMS), spinal haematoma (urgent MRI if new deficit), pulmonary embolism, ileus (opioid + immobility)

anaesthesia.preferred: EARLY INTUBATION if any airway concern + aggressive fluid resuscitation per Parkland + concurrent escharotomy if circumferential burn (per ABA / Advanced Burn Life Support 2024)
considerations: ═══ IMMEDIATE PRIORITIES (FIRST 30 MIN) ═══

A — AIRWAY: intubate EARLY (before swelling) if any of: facial burn, singed nasal hair, soot in nares/sputum, hoarseness, stridor, closed-space fire, deep neck burn, GCS < 8, > 30 % TBSA, anticipated long transport
Use largest ETT possible (anticipate need for repeated bronchoscopy in inhalation injury); cuffed; secure with CLOTH TIES around head (adhesive tape will not stick)
Document tube position; accidental extubation in oedematous airway = catastrophic

B — BREATHING: 100 % FiO₂ until COHb < 5 % (half-life 4–6 h room air, 60–90 min 100 % O₂, 20–30 min hyperbaric); ABG with co-oximetry; suspect cyanide toxicity in unexplained lactic acidosis from house fire — hydroxocobalamin 5 g IV adult / 70 mg/kg paeds
Circumferential chest burn → escharotomy for chest wall expansion (life-saving)
C — CIRCULATION: 2 large-bore IVs (through burned skin OK if needed); IO if access difficult; foley for hourly UO; arterial line for serial ABG
D — DISABILITY: GCS, glucose, pupil, lateralising signs (associated injuries common in explosion/fall)
E — EXPOSURE: assess TBSA (Lund-Browder for paeds — age-stratified head/limb proportions), depth, depth of burn; head-to-toe for occult trauma
═══ TBSA ASSESSMENT ═══
Adult: Wallace rule of nines OR Lund-Browder (more accurate especially for small burns)
Paediatric: Lund-Browder MANDATORY (infant head = 18 % vs adult 9 %; legs proportionally smaller in young)
EXCLUDE epidermal (simple erythema) from TBSA calculation; INCLUDE partial-thickness and full-thickness only
═══ FLUID RESUSCITATION — MODIFIED PARKLAND (ABA 2024) ═══
Threshold for IV resuscitation: adult > 15 % TBSA; paeds > 10 % TBSA

ADULT: 2–4 mL/kg/% TBSA Lactated Ringer over 24 h (start with 3 mL/kg/% — historical 4 mL associated with "fluid creep" + ARDS); HALF in first 8 h (from TIME OF INJURY, not arrival), HALF in next 16 h
PAEDIATRIC: 3–4 mL/kg/% TBSA Lactated Ringer PLUS maintenance (Holliday-Segar — children < 30 kg need dextrose-containing maintenance because of limited glycogen stores)
• 4 mL/kg/h for first 10 kg + 2 mL/kg/h for 10–20 kg + 1 mL/kg/h for each kg > 20
• Use D5 ½ NS or D5 LR for maintenance
INHALATION INJURY: +30–50 % fluid
ELECTRICAL: 4–9 mL/kg/% TBSA; target UO 1.5–2 mL/kg/h (rhabdomyolysis/myoglobin clearance)
TITRATE TO UO (not formula alone): adult 0.5–1 mL/kg/h; paeds 1–2 mL/kg/h; electrical 1.5–2 mL/kg/h
Adjust ± 10–20 % every hour based on UO; AVOID over-resuscitation ("fluid creep" → ARDS, abdominal compartment syndrome, extremity compartment syndrome)
After first 24 h: maintenance + replacement, add albumin 5 % to keep albumin > 20 g/L
═══ ESCHAROTOMY (PROCEDURAL) ═══

Indications: circumferential full-thickness burns of chest (impairs ventilation), abdomen (raised intra-abdominal pressure), or extremity (compartment syndrome — distal pulses lost, increasing compartment pressure)

CAN be done at bedside with minimal anaesthesia — burned skin has destroyed nerve fibres in full-thickness areas (LITFL); typically light sedation + opioid; deep partial-thickness areas need more analgesia (intact nerves)
If extensive or paediatric → OR + GA + ETT (avoid sux > 24 h post-burn — see paed-burns/burn-debridement)
═══ ANALGESIA — HIGH-DOSE ═══
Morphine 0.1 mg/kg IV titrated; ketamine 0.5 mg/kg IV bolus + 0.15–0.3 mg/kg/h infusion (multimodal); fentanyl bolus for procedures
Anxiolysis: midazolam 1–2 mg adult / 0.05–0.1 mg/kg paeds — caution with hypotension
═══ TEMPERATURE — CRITICAL ═══
Burns lose massive heat (no skin barrier); warm everything (theatre to 32 °C if surgical, ICU room ≥ 28 °C, forced-air warmer, fluid warmer, warmed irrigation, head cover)
Target core ≥ 36.5 °C; hypothermia → coagulopathy + arrhythmia + delayed wound healing
═══ INHALATION INJURY MANAGEMENT ═══
Diagnosis: history (closed-space, smoke, steam), exam (soot, singed hair, stridor, hoarseness, sputum), bronchoscopy (gold standard — soot below cords confirms)
Treatment: humidified O₂, nebulised heparin 5000 U + NAC 3 mL 20 % q4h (CONTROVERSIAL but in many protocols), bronchodilators, suction
COHb > 25 % symptomatic or > 15 % in pregnancy: consider hyperbaric O₂ if available
CYANIDE TOXICITY (unexplained lactic acidosis post-fire): hydroxocobalamin 5 g IV adult / 70 mg/kg paeds (preferred over sodium thiosulphate which is slow)
═══ INVESTIGATIONS ═══

ABG + co-oximetry (COHb, MetHb), CBC, U&E, glucose, lactate, CK (rhabdo if electrical/deep), coagulation, group & save, CXR (often clear initially → infiltrates day 2 if inhalation), ECG (electrical burns → arrhythmia risk × 24–48 h)

considerations: ═══ PATIENT POPULATION ═══

End-stage HF (ischaemic, dilated CMP, valvular, hypertrophic, congenital, restrictive); often on chronic inotropes (dobutamine/milrinone) and/or mechanical support (LVAD, ECMO, Impella, IABP) as bridge to transplant

PAEDIATRIC: most common indications = congenital heart disease (single ventricle, complex anatomy after multiple palliations), cardiomyopathy (dilated, hypertrophic, restrictive), retransplant; smaller donor pool → longer wait times

Pre-existing pulmonary HTN: most concerning predictor of post-transplant primary graft dysfunction (PVR > 5 Wood units = high risk; > 7 Wood units = relative contraindication unless reversible on dobutamine/iNO trial)
Recipient size-matching: donor:recipient body weight ratio 0.8–1.5 acceptable; oversized donor → bradycardia + tamponade-like physiology; undersized donor → RV failure, especially if recipient PHT
═══ PRE-OP COORDINATION ═══
Coordinate with retrieval team: cold ischaemic time matters (4–6 h acceptable; > 6 h = increased PGD); donor heart on ice in cooler until anastomosis
Confirm: donor + recipient ABO compatibility, HLA crossmatch, CMV/EBV serology, last dialysis (if HD-dependent), recent infections (immunosuppression starting)
Reverse anticoagulation if on warfarin (4F-PCC + vit K) or DOAC (idarucizumab / andexanet alfa)
Cross-match 4–6 PRBC + FFP + platelets; cell salvage; MTP ready; redo sternotomy more common → extra blood + perfusionist alert for emergent CPB at sternotomy
═══ INDUCTION — FAILING HEART ═══
Arterial line + vasopressor support BEFORE induction (radial pre-induction, femoral added by surgeon when scrubbed)
Continue chronic inotrope infusions through induction (dobutamine, milrinone)
Etomidate 0.2–0.3 mg/kg + fentanyl 5–10 mcg/kg + slow propofol titration (avoid large bolus)
Ketamine acceptable (preserves SVR + contractility); paeds may need sevoflurane induction if no IV access
Rocuronium 1.2 mg/kg (or vecuronium); avoid sux if recent dialysis / hyperkalaemia
═══ CPB CONDUCT ═══
Redo sternotomy precautions: peripheral access for emergent CPB (femoral cannulation if RV/great vessel injury at re-entry); cell salvage; large-bore venous return
Heparin 300–400 U/kg (ACT > 480 s); TXA 30 mg/kg load + 16 mg/kg/h infusion
Standard CPB conduct; donor heart implanted with bicaval (preferred over biatrial — preserves atrial function and reduces TR)
═══ DONOR HEART ISCHAEMIC TIME ═══
Cold ischaemic time (CIT): cross-clamp release of donor to recipient unclamp; target < 4 h, acceptable < 6 h
Warm ischaemic time minimised by surgeon technique
Reperfusion injury graded by primary graft dysfunction (PGD) — see below
═══ WEANING FROM CPB ═══
Use VA-CPB-WEAN checklist (see CPB weaning section); SPECIFIC additions for transplant:
DENERVATED HEART: no neural reflexes — no Bainbridge, no baroreceptor compensation, no vagal tone
• Atropine INEFFECTIVE for bradycardia (no vagal innervation to block) — use ISOPRENALINE infusion 0.01–0.1 mcg/kg/min OR direct epicardial PACING (often inserted prophylactically)
• Adrenaline + dopamine retain effects (direct β1)
• Heart rate target 90–110 (sinus or paced) — denervated heart depends on preload (Frank-Starling) and intrinsic rate
• Drugs requiring sympathetic preservation are blunted (ephedrine partial effect)
• Avoid neostigmine without anticholinergic (NO vagal effect anyway, so glycopyrrolate sufficient)
PULMONARY VASODILATOR from start: iNO 20–40 ppm OR nebulised epoprostenol; reduces RV afterload on the new heart
Inotropic support: adrenaline 0.05–0.1 mcg/kg/min + milrinone 0.375–0.75 mcg/kg/min (almost always needed)
═══ PRIMARY GRAFT DYSFUNCTION (PGD) — MAJOR THREAT ═══

Definition: ISHLT 2014 grading (Kobashigawa Delphi consensus) — updated by ISHLT April 2024 consensus conference (recognising vasoplegia frequently co-exists with PGD; current risk-stratification tools have limitations)
LV / RV / both ventricular dysfunction within 24 h of transplant, not attributable to surgical / immunological / known causes
PGD-3 (severe): requires mechanical circulatory support → 30 % mortality at 30 days; leading cause of early death post-transplant
Risk factors: prolonged ischaemic time (> 4 h), oversized recipient, donor inotrope use, recipient PHT, mechanical bridge to transplant, female donor → male recipient
INTRAOP RECOGNITION: failure to wean from CPB despite optimised pharmacology; TEE shows hypocontractile graft; rising LAP / CVP; falling MAP / CI
TREATMENT: re-establish CPB → reassess → if persistent → VA-ECMO (central or peripheral) → bridge to recovery (24–96 h typical), retransplant or transition to durable VAD if no recovery
═══ POST-CPB / PROTAMINE ═══
Slow protamine ≥ 10 min; reversal-related vasoplegia common in transplant (pre-existing inflammation + immunosuppression onset)

Vasoplegia management: noradrenaline + vasopressin → methylene blue 1–2 mg/kg refractory (excellent rescue in cardiac transplant per multiple case series; CAUTION if patient on anti-PAH drugs e.g. sildenafil/riociguat — drug interactions; AVOID if G6PD deficiency, serotonergic drugs like SSRIs — risk of serotonin syndrome)

Hydroxocobalamin 5 g IV over 15 min: emerging 2nd-line for MB-refractory vasoplegia (per Pai 2024 Clin Transplant) — works via NO scavenging like MB but different binding; useful if MB contraindicated; may cause red urine + interfere with colorimetric lab tests (bilirubin, creatinine)
Coagulation: ROTEM-guided; very high transfusion + bleeding rate (redo + coagulopathy + heparin); platelets often needed (chronic HF → platelet dysfunction)
═══ IMMUNOSUPPRESSION (INTRA-OP START) ═══
Induction: methylprednisolone 1 g IV at aortic cross-clamp release (paeds 10 mg/kg, max 1 g); basiliximab 20 mg IV (or ATG per centre); CMV-negative blood products if seronegative recipient
Continued post-op: tacrolimus + MMF + steroid taper per centre protocol
STRICT STERILE PRECAUTIONS (immunosuppression starting) — full surgical PPE, sterile technique for all lines, dedicated equipment
═══ PAEDIATRIC-SPECIFIC ═══
Smaller volumes → relatively more transfusion per kg; rapid haemodynamic swings
Heart rate priorities higher (paeds CO more rate-dependent): target HR 110–150 infant, 100–130 child, 90–120 adolescent
PHT more reversible than adult — iNO trial pre-op often successful in reducing PVR
Single ventricle physiology (Fontan circulation pre-transplant) — relatively dehydrated, vulnerable to induction agents; ketamine + low-dose propofol preferred
Delayed sternal closure common (size discrepancy + tissue oedema)
TEE limited by probe size in small infants — epicardial echo by cardiology team
═══ POST-OP ═══
CICU intubated 24–72 h typically; longer if PGD, paeds, delayed sternal closure
Doppler hourly × 24 h for graft thrombosis (cardiology / TTE)
Endomyocardial biopsy: first protocol biopsy day 7–10 post-op (rejection screening)
CMV / EBV / fungal prophylaxis per centre
Driveline / line infections, AKI, neurological events, rejection — surveillance
