Adult 30 mg/kg load + 16 mg/kg/h; paeds 10 mg/kg + 1 mg/kg/h

name: Anterior mediastinal mass resection (lymphoma / thymoma / teratoma)

options: GA — high-risk: maintain spontaneous ventilation, avoid muscle relaxants, awake fibreoptic if symptomatic
anaesthesia.preferred: Risk-stratified: asymptomatic + small → standard GA; symptomatic / > 50% tracheal cross-section reduction / SVC compression → AWAKE FOI + spontaneous ventilation, femoral CPB on standby
considerations: HIGH-STAKES — anterior mediastinal mass can cause cardiopulmonary collapse on induction (loss of muscle tone unmasks airway/great vessel compression)
Pre-op assessment: dyspnoea positional? cough? SVC syndrome? syncope? supine intolerance?
CT chest mandatory — measure tracheal cross-sectional area (> 50% narrowing = high risk), bronchial compression, great vessel/cardiac involvement
Echo: pericardial effusion, cardiac tamponade, vessel compression
PFTs (flow-volume loops upright + supine — variable extrathoracic vs intrathoracic pattern)
High-risk plan: AWAKE fibreoptic intubation in lateral or sitting position, MAINTAIN SPONTANEOUS VENTILATION throughout, AVOID muscle relaxants until airway secured beyond obstruction
Have rigid bronchoscope ready, femoral CPB / ECMO on standby with surgeon scrubbed for very high-risk
IV access in lower limb if SVC compression (drugs may not reach heart from upper limb)
Position changes (lateral) may relieve OR worsen compression — find best position before induction
For paediatric: same principles, even more critical (smaller airway, mass effect proportionally larger)
Lymphoma: pre-op steroids may reduce mass urgently (but interferes with histological diagnosis — discuss with oncology)

options: GA + cross-field ventilation through surgical-field tube
anaesthesia.preferred: GA + CONVENTIONAL ETT initially → cross-field intubation through surgical incision once trachea opened → reconnect ETT after anastomosis
considerations: Shared airway emergency potential — multidisciplinary planning essential
Pre-op flexible bronchoscopy to measure stenosis/tumour position
Reinforced ETT, smaller size than usual
During open phase: surgeon takes airway with sterile field tube, ventilation continues distally
Head + neck flexion post-op (chin-to-chest sutures often used) — DO NOT extend neck (anastomotic dehiscence)
Extubate awake with patient sitting + neck flexed
Post-op anastomotic leak / dehiscence is feared — soft diet, no PPV via mask, no head extension
If reintubation needed → fibreoptic, do not pass ETT cuff across anastomosis

name: Decortication / pleurectomy for empyema or trapped lung

options: GA + DLT + thoracic epidural T6–T8 OR paravertebral catheter
anaesthesia.preferred: GA + DLT + thoracic epidural OR paravertebral catheter
considerations: Often septic (empyema) — sepsis bundle, broad-spectrum antibiotics
Underlying disease: TB, post-pneumonia, malignancy, post-surgical
Trapped lung — trapped/restricted volume, ventilation difficult on affected side
OLV essential — DLT confirmation with bronchoscope
Bleeding from chest wall + pleural surface can be substantial
Severe post-op pain — uncontrolled → atelectasis, pneumonia
Air leak common post-op — chest drains
High risk of post-op respiratory failure if marginal lung function

options: GA + arterial line + CVC + TEE + cooling for CPB
anaesthesia.preferred: GA + arterial line (radial/femoral) + CVC + TEE
considerations: TOF physiology: VSD + RV outflow obstruction + overriding aorta + RV hypertrophy → R-to-L shunt (cyanosis)
"Tet spell" precipitants: crying, pain, hypovolaemia, low SVR → MORE R-to-L shunt → worsening cyanosis
Tet spell management: knees-to-chest, 100% O₂, fluid bolus 10–20 mL/kg, phenylephrine 1–10 mcg/kg, morphine 0.1 mg/kg, esmolol 0.5 mg/kg, sodium bicarbonate, deepen anaesthesia
AVOID drops in SVR (excessive volatile, vasodilators) — increases R-to-L shunt
AVOID tachycardia (worsens dynamic RVOT obstruction) — beta-blocker if sinus tachycardia
Maintain preload + SVR — fluid loading + phenylephrine ready
Ketamine acceptable for induction (preserves SVR) — historical concerns about RVOT spasm overstated
Air filters on all IV lines — paradoxical air embolism through R-to-L shunt
CPB via ascending aorta + bicaval cannulation, repair: VSD closure + RVOT relief (transannular patch / valve-sparing)
Post-CPB: residual VSD, RV dysfunction, pulmonary regurgitation common
TEE for residual lesions
ICU post-op, ventilated, often delayed sternal closure if oedema
Modified ultrafiltration (MUF) at end of CPB to reduce inflammation/oedema
Antifibrinolytics (TXA / aprotinin where available)

surgerySpecificDrugs.dose: 1–10 mcg/kg IV bolus or 0.1–0.5 mcg/kg/min infusion
1 mg per 100 U heparin (paed cap proportional)

options: Neonatal GA + arterial line + CVC + TEE + CPB
anaesthesia.preferred: Neonatal GA — narcotic-based (high-dose fentanyl 25–50 mcg/kg) + muscle relaxant + low-dose volatile
considerations: Neonatal cardiac surgery — usually first 2 weeks of life
TGA physiology: aorta from RV, pulmonary artery from LV → two parallel circulations; survival depends on mixing (PFO/PDA/VSD)
Pre-op prostaglandin E1 infusion to maintain PDA (0.01–0.05 mcg/kg/min) — apnoea risk, intubate before transfer
Balloon atrial septostomy (Rashkind) often performed in cath lab to enlarge inter-atrial communication
Critical preoperative SpO₂ usually 70–85% (mixing-dependent)
Coronary artery transfer is the highest-risk step — myocardial ischaemia possible
Neonatal CPB — small volumes, deep hypothermia (18–25°C), pH-stat strategy
Modified ultrafiltration mandatory
High-dose fentanyl + relaxant attenuates stress response
Coagulopathy frequent — platelets, FFP, cryoprecipitate, fibrinogen often needed
Post-op: open sternum often, ICU ventilated, inotropes (milrinone, adrenaline)
Mortality ~3–5% in experienced centres

options: GA + arterial line + CVC + TEE + CPB
anaesthesia.preferred: GA + arterial line + CVC + TEE
considerations: Final stage of single-ventricle palliation (after Norwood + Glenn)
Fontan physiology: passive flow from systemic veins → pulmonary arteries (no sub-pulmonary ventricle)
"Fontan paradox": BOTH preload-dependent AND afterload-dependent — needs adequate filling AND low PVR
AVOID: high airway pressures (impedes pulmonary flow), hypovolaemia, pulmonary HTN, acidosis, hypoxia, tachycardia, low SVR
Ventilation: low Vt, low PEEP (or none), short inspiratory time, spontaneous ventilation when possible (negative-pressure → enhances Fontan flow)
Maintain SR (atrial contraction important)
Hepatic congestion + protein-losing enteropathy + Fontan-associated liver disease in older Fontans
Anticoagulation chronic (warfarin / aspirin) — manage perioperatively
Pulmonary vasodilators (NO, sildenafil) post-op
High mortality if Fontan fails — consider redo / heart transplant referral

options: GA via ETT (lateral thoracotomy) ± arterial line
anaesthesia.preferred: GA + appropriate-size ETT + arterial line if neonate/unstable
considerations: Often preterm neonate — multiple comorbidities (RDS, IVH, NEC, immature thermoregulation)
Bedside in NICU preferred for unstable preterm — avoid transfer
Lateral position — left lung down (right lung ventilated)
OLV usually NOT needed — surgeon retracts lung
Aorta + pulmonary artery + recurrent laryngeal nerve close to ductus — surgeon caution
Transient HTN at clipping (loss of run-off)
Test ligation: oxygenation should improve, pulmonary pressures drop
Avoid: hypothermia (preterm), hypoglycaemia, hyperoxia (ROP/BPD risk in preterm)
Apnoea risk post-op in preterm — monitor in NICU
Older child: VATS or interventional closure (cath lab) preferred over open

anaesthesia.preferred: GA + lumbar/caudal epidural + arterial line + CVC
considerations: Pre-op chemotherapy (vincristine + actinomycin ± doxorubicin per SIOP protocol) — anaemia, neutropenia, neuropathy, cardiotoxicity
Doxorubicin → check echo (LVEF)
Tumour size often massive relative to child — may displace IVC, push diaphragm up (impaired ventilation)
Pre-op imaging: tumour extent, IVC tumour thrombus possible (5–10%), bilateral disease
Tumour rupture / spillage = upstaging — careful handling, avoid abdominal compression
Vincristine peripheral neuropathy — careful positioning, document baseline
Hypertension common (renin-mediated) — control pre-op
Resection: nephrectomy ± thrombectomy ± vena cava reconstruction (if IVC thrombus)
Massive bleeding possible — large IVs × 2, blood ready
WAGR syndrome / Beckwith-Wiedemann associations — macroglossia, hypoglycaemia (Beckwith)
ICU/HDU post-op

options: GA + epidural / regional + arterial line + CVC
anaesthesia.preferred: GA + appropriate regional (caudal/epidural for abdominal, paravertebral for thoracic) + arterial line + CVC
considerations: Catecholamine-secreting tumour — like a phaeochromocytoma in a child
Pre-op urinary VMA / HVA + plasma metanephrines
Hypertension common — alpha-blockade (phenoxybenzamine) for at least 5–7 days pre-op IF symptomatic / catecholamine-positive
BP swings on tumour manipulation — same drugs as phaeo (phentolamine, magnesium, SNP, GTN)
Post-tumour-ligation: hypotension — fluid + noradrenaline
Pre-op chemo (cisplatin, etoposide, vincristine, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin) — multi-organ toxicity
Often advanced disease at presentation — bone marrow involvement (pancytopenia), liver disease
Paraspinal / dumbbell tumours may extend into spinal canal — neurology baseline, careful regional
MIBG-positive tumour — radiopharmaceutical scan history (no anaesthetic interaction)
ICU post-op

name: Paediatric posterior fossa tumour resection (medulloblastoma / ependymoma)

options: GA TIVA (or balanced) + arterial line + CVC + neuromonitoring
anaesthesia.preferred: GA TIVA (propofol + remifentanil) + arterial line + CVC + neuromonitoring
considerations: Most common location for paediatric brain tumours
Hydrocephalus from 4th ventricle obstruction — raised ICP, often shunt or EVD pre-op
Posterior fossa = brainstem proximity → cranial nerve dysfunction risk, autonomic instability
Position: prone OR sitting — sitting carries air embolism risk (precordial Doppler/CVC, TEE if available, treat per protocol)
Prone position more common in paediatric (lower air embolism risk, better access)
Neuromonitoring (BAEP, SSEP, cranial nerve EMG) — TIVA mandatory (avoid volatile/N₂O/NMBA after intubation)
Bradycardia from brainstem manipulation — atropine ready, warn surgeon
Cushing reflex (HTN + bradycardia) = brainstem compression — communicate to surgeon
Post-op posterior fossa syndrome (cerebellar mutism) common after midline lesion resection
Smooth emergence — cough/strain → haemorrhage / oedema
ICU post-op with neuro-obs
Pre-op chemo / RT (older children) considerations

anaesthesia.preferred: GA + epidural + arterial line + CVC + low CVP technique
considerations: Most common paediatric liver malignancy (< 3 years typical)
Pre-op chemo (PLADO: cisplatin + doxorubicin) — cardiotoxicity, nephrotoxicity, ototoxicity
AFP marker — falls with treatment
Same principles as adult major hepatectomy: low CVP, Pringle manoeuvre, air embolism risk
Coagulopathy if extensive resection (transient liver dysfunction)
Massive bleeding possible — group & crossmatch, blood ready
Liver transplant alternative if unresectable — consider transplant centre referral
ICU post-op, monitor for post-hepatectomy liver failure (bilirubin + INR day 5)
Anchored with arterial + CVC for prolonged surgery

name: Bone marrow harvest (donor) — paediatric or adult

anaesthesia.preferred: Adult: spinal + sedation; paediatric: GA + LMA (PIH/iliac aspiration)
considerations: Donor — usually healthy, but ethical considerations (paediatric sibling donor)
Iliac crest aspiration in prone position (multiple punctures)
Volume harvested 10–20 mL/kg recipient weight (max 1500 mL adult donor) — replace with crystalloid + autologous blood pre-banked
Pre-op autologous blood donation 1–2 weeks pre-op for replacement
Post-op pain in iliac region — multimodal (paracetamol, NSAID if no CI, opioid sparingly)
Day-case feasible in adults; overnight in paediatric
Counsel donor: pain, fatigue 1–2 weeks; no long-term sequelae
PBSC (peripheral blood stem cell) harvest is alternative — apheresis after G-CSF priming, no anaesthesia needed

options: GA + appropriate ETT (3.0–3.5 mm uncuffed) + arterial line + caudal/epidural
anaesthesia.preferred: GA + spontaneous-assisted ventilation initially → IPPV after fistula ligation; arterial line; caudal catheter
considerations: Neonatal emergency surgery — typically day 2–4 of life
Type C (proximal atresia + distal fistula) most common (85%)
Pre-op: NG tube on continuous suction (Replogle), head-up 30°, IV antibiotics, IV fluids
Pre-op echo to rule out VACTERL associations: Vertebral, Anal, Cardiac (30%, e.g. VSD/TOF), TE-fistula, Renal, Limb
CRITICAL induction problem: positive-pressure ventilation can blow gas through the fistula → gastric distension → splints diaphragm → ventilation impossible
Strategies to avoid this: (1) keep spontaneous ventilation until fistula ligated, (2) careful low-pressure mask ventilation, (3) intubate with tip BELOW fistula (bronchoscope-guided ETT placement)
Right thoracotomy left-lateral position — left lung ventilated (single-lung physiology in neonate)
Bronchoscopy by surgeon at start to identify fistula location
Hypoxia common during retraction — communicate, intermittent reinflation
Post-op: ICU ventilated, NG tube, no blind suction (anastomosis), avoid extending neck
Anastomotic leak / stricture common late complication

options: Neonatal GA + arterial line + CVC (umbilical) + gentle ventilation
Adjunct: erector spinae plane block (open) or wound infiltration (thoracoscopic)
anaesthesia.preferred: Neonatal GA + arterial line (preductal — right radial) + CVC (umbilical or femoral) + gentle ventilation + opioid-based + ESP/wound LA
considerations: Pre-op stabilisation (mean 5–10 days, sometimes weeks) before delayed elective repair — DO NOT operate on the unstable neonate. Indicators of stability: PaCO₂ < 60 mmHg with PIP < 28, FiO₂ < 0.50, normal pre-ductal saturations, lactate < 3, no pulmonary hypertensive crises (CDH EURO Consortium 2016, updated guidance)
Pulmonary hypoplasia + abnormal pulmonary vasculature are the lethal pathologies — closure of the defect does NOT improve lung function immediately and may worsen it short-term
AT BIRTH: do NOT bag-mask (inflates GI tract → splints lung); intubate immediately in delivery suite, decompress with OG tube on continuous suction

CDH EURO Consortium ventilation strategy: Vt 4–5 mL/kg, PIP < 25 cmH₂O (target ≤ 25; never > 28), PEEP 3–5 cmH₂O, RR 40–60. Permissive hypercapnia: PaCO₂ up to 60–70 mmHg accepted PROVIDED pH > 7.20. HFOV considered when conventional ventilation requires PIP > 28 or MAP > 15
Pre-ductal SpO₂ target 85–95% (preductal = R radial; reflects cerebral oxygenation upstream of any R→L shunt at the duct)
Avoid high FiO₂ (oxygen toxicity + reactive PVR rebound) — titrate to preductal SpO₂; aggressive weaning

PHTN management: milrinone (inodilator, lowers PVR — first-line); sildenafil; vasopressin for systemic SVR support if combined LV dysfunction. iNO has NOT shown mortality benefit in CDH (NICHD trials, NEOPAIN)— use only as rescue or temporising agent before ECMO; do not include in routine bundle
Position: supine; ~90% Bochdalek defects are LEFT-sided
Avoid N₂O (expands hollow viscus)
Avoid abrupt PVR-raising stimuli: pain (deep opioid), hypoxia, hypercarbia > target, acidosis, hypothermia, agitation
Surgical approach: open transabdominal vs thoracoscopic — thoracoscopy needs CO₂ insufflation (worsens hypercapnia + acidosis), reserved for stable infants only
ECMO criteria: failure of optimal medical management with PaO₂ < 60 mmHg pre-ductal, pH < 7.15, lactate > 5 — early consultation, do not delay
Post-op: ICU ventilated, gradual wean over days; mortality 20–30% in severe cases (observed/expected lung volume < 25%, liver-up)

surgerySpecificDrugs.indication: Stress response attenuation, blunt PVR rises

surgerySpecificDrugs.dose: 0.5–2 mg/kg PO q6h (oral) or 0.4 mg/kg IV q8h

surgerySpecificDrugs.indication: Systemic SVR support in vasoplegia + PHTN combination
PHTN rescue ONLY (no mortality benefit in CDH per NICHD; bridge to ECMO)
surgerySpecificDrugs.dose: 20 ppm starting; wean as PVR settles

options: GA + RSI (modified) + ETT + local infiltration ± caudal
anaesthesia.preferred: GA + RSI with ETT (full stomach despite NPO) + local infiltration by surgeon
considerations: Pyloric stenosis is a MEDICAL emergency, NOT a surgical one — fluid + electrolyte correction MUST precede surgery (BJA Education 2018; OpenAnesthesia 2024)
Classic biochemistry: hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic METABOLIC ALKALOSIS (loss of gastric HCl from projectile vomiting); paradoxical aciduria late
Resuscitation: 0.9% saline 20 mL/kg bolus then 1.5–2× maintenance with 5% dextrose / 0.45% saline + KCl 10–20 mmol/L (added once urine output established)

Pre-op correction targets (BJA Educ 2018 ranges): pH 7.30–7.45, Cl⁻ > 100 mmol/L, HCO₃⁻ < 30 mmol/L, base excess −4 to +2.5, K⁺ 3.5–5.5; urine output > 1 mL/kg/h; classically takes 24–48 h, severe cases 5–10 days
Bedside gastric USS (antral cross-section) recommended pre-induction to assess gastric residuum; empty stomach via OG/NG tube in supine, right-lateral, left-lateral positions before induction
WHY correction matters: persistent CSF alkalosis → central respiratory depression + post-op apnoea even after serum pH normalised
NECTARINE 2022 (Disma, Br J Anaesth, PMID 36064492): pyloric stenosis neonates have INCREASED rate of difficult airway management — anticipate, prepare videolaryngoscope and Plan B

Modified RSI: pre-oxygenate, gentle face-mask ventilation acceptable (low pressures, avoid gastric inflation), cricoid pressure controversial in infants (may distort airway), ETT (cuffed micro-cuff or uncuffed appropriate-size)
Maintenance: sevoflurane + air/O₂ + opioid-sparing analgesia (paracetamol + LA infiltration ± caudal); deep extubation acceptable when alkalosis fully corrected
AVOID morphine + benzodiazepines in infant (apnoea + bradycardia risk) — paracetamol + wound infiltration are sufficient
Post-op feeding: ad libitum or graded feeds within 4 h are now both supported (Hong 2021, Pediatr Surg Int)
Apnoea monitoring 24 h post-op (especially preterm or co-existing respiratory illness); day-case discharge possible from 6 h with parents in selected centres

surgerySpecificDrugs.dose: 0.9% saline 20 mL/kg bolus, then 1.5–2× maintenance (5% dextrose / 0.45% NaCl + KCl)

conditional: Diagnostic abdominal USS (pyloric muscle thickness > 3–4 mm, channel length > 15–19 mm)

options: GA + south-facing oral RAE ETT + throat pack + maxillary block
anaesthesia.preferred: GA + south-facing oral RAE ETT (taped to chin, fixed midline) + throat pack + bilateral maxillary nerve block
considerations: Typically 9–18 months age (later than cleft lip at 3–4 months)
Difficult airway — micrognathia common, especially in syndromic (Pierre Robin, Treacher Collins)
Pierre Robin sequence: micrognathia + glossoptosis + cleft palate → very difficult intubation
Inhalation induction common, secure airway before NMBA
South-facing RAE tube fixed midline (surgeon needs midline access)
Boyle-Davis gag distorts airway — frequent ETT dislodgement, breath sound check after positioning
Throat pack mandatory (blood) — tag and document removal
Bilateral maxillary nerve block (suprazygomatic approach) — excellent post-op analgesia
Avoid NSAIDs in some centres (bleeding risk on raw mucosa) — local practice
Avoid morphine in young infant — fentanyl titrated
Post-op: nurse prone or lateral, no pacifier/no oral suction blind, no NG tube for 1 week
Tongue stitch by surgeon (some centres) — lifeline if airway obstruction post-op
Syndromic infant → ICU post-op (Pierre Robin, Treacher Collins)

surgerySpecificDrugs.dose: 0.25% bupivacaine 0.15 mL/kg per side (max 0.5 mg/kg total)

options: GA + ETT (south-facing oral RAE) + throat pack
anaesthesia.preferred: GA + south-facing oral RAE ETT with throat pack — most centres
considerations: Common indication: OSA (apnoea, snoring, mouth breathing) — pre-op sleep study desirable
OSA children are EXQUISITELY sensitive to opioids → use minimal + multimodal
Avoid morphine in OSA child < 3 years; use fentanyl + paracetamol + dexamethasone + LA
Severe OSA / age < 3 / syndromic → ICU/HDU post-op, NOT day-case
Boyle-Davis gag distorts airway — frequent dislodgement, recheck breath sounds
Throat pack mandatory — tag and document removal
Dexamethasone 0.15–0.5 mg/kg = 2-fold benefit (PONV + analgesia + airway oedema)
PONV very common — triple anti-emetic (dex + ondansetron + propofol TIVA)
Smooth deep extubation OR fully awake — never in stage 2
Post-op observation 4 h minimum
Post-tonsillectomy bleeding: PRIMARY (< 24 h, minor) or SECONDARY (5–10 days, can be major) → see emergency tonsillectomy bleed

options: GA + RSI (classical apneic OR controlled with gentle mask vent < 12 cmH₂O) + ETT + 2 large IVs
anaesthesia.preferred: GA + controlled RSI with gentle mask ventilation < 12 cmH₂O (current evidence-based — Lee & Haché 2022) + ETT + IV access × 2 + crossmatched blood available
considerations: Reference: Lee & Haché 2022 (Int J Gen Med); Fields et al 2010 (Paediatr Anaesth); OpenAnesthesia PTH 2023
EMERGENCY — child has been bleeding hours, often UNDERESTIMATED blood loss; swallowed blood masks true volume
Hypovolaemia presentation: tachycardia (compensatory), capillary refill > 3 sec, lethargy, pallor — children compensate until ~ 40% blood volume lost, then crash
KEY EVIDENCE-INSIGHT: Hypoxia is more common than aspiration in PTH (Fields 2010 — 9.9% transient hypoxia vs ~ 0% aspiration)

Pre-op resuscitation MANDATORY before induction: IV access × 2 (large bore — IO if difficult), fluid bolus 20 mL/kg crystalloid (warmed), group-specific or crossmatched blood IN ROOM, correct coagulopathy if FFP available
Type & screen → crossmatched RBC ideally before induction (don't induce on dropping Hb)
AIRWAY HAZARDS: full stomach (swallowed blood — large volume in stomach), ongoing bleeding into pharynx obscures laryngoscopy view, post-op tissue swelling

PRE-INDUCTION SETUP: 2 working suction units (one Yankauer, one fine-bore), multiple ETT sizes (one size smaller than original tonsillectomy), video laryngoscope + fibreoptic, surgeon scrubbed and ready for surgical airway as rescue
PREOXYGENATION: in left lateral decubitus head-down position if cooperative (allows blood drainage); supine if uncooperative
INDUCTION CHOICE — TWO ACCEPTED APPROACHES:
1. CLASSICAL APNEIC RSI: cricoid pressure + induction agent + NMBA + intubate without ventilation (traditional aspiration prevention)
2. CONTROLLED RSI with gentle mask ventilation < 12 cmH₂O (Kemper 2018, Lee 2022): less hypoxaemia, better laryngoscopy view, low aspiration risk in venous oozing — increasingly recommended

INDUCTION DRUGS: KETAMINE 1–2 mg/kg (preserves CO in hypovolaemia, first-line); etomidate 0.2–0.3 mg/kg acceptable; AVOID propofol bolus full-dose (cardiovascular collapse); reduce all doses by 30–50% in shocked child
NMBA: suxamethonium 1.5–2 mg/kg (fastest, classical) OR rocuronium 1–1.2 mg/kg (sugammadex MUST be available for rescue)
TXA 15 mg/kg IV at induction reasonable (low-evidence but guideline-supported; e.g. Iowa protocol)
NG TUBE after intubation to decompress stomach (large amount of swallowed blood) — do not pass before intubation (vomiting risk)
AVOID extubation in deep plane (re-bleed/laryngospasm) — fully awake extubation in left lateral position; have suction immediately ready
Post-op: HDU/PICU 12–24 h observation (re-bleed risk, ongoing fluid resuscitation, post-extubation airway watch)

surgerySpecificDrugs.dose: 20 mL/kg over 10–15 min, repeat to clinical response

surgerySpecificDrugs.indication: Induction agent of choice (preserves CO in hypovolaemia)
Rocuronium reversal — MUST be drawn up if rocuronium used
Massive transfusion if loss > 30% blood volume
surgerySpecificDrugs.dose: PRBC 10–20 mL/kg + FFP 10 mL/kg + platelets 10 mL/kg in 1:1:1 ratio

conditional: Bleeding history — von Willebrand screen if recurrent

options: Neonatal GA + arterial line + caudal ± epidural
anaesthesia.preferred: Neonatal GA + arterial line + caudal block; staged silo + delayed primary closure for very large defects
considerations: Neonatal emergency — surgery within hours of birth (gastroschisis) or staged (large omphalocele)
Pre-op heat loss massive (exposed bowel) — humidified silo bag, warm fluids, warming devices
Fluid losses massive — 2–3× maintenance, monitor electrolytes
OMPHALOCELE: covered by membrane, often syndromic (Beckwith-Wiedemann, trisomy 13/18, congenital cardiac in 30%) → echo mandatory
GASTROSCHISIS: typically isolated, exposed bowel, NO membrane, usually no associated anomalies
Beckwith-Wiedemann → macroglossia (difficult airway), hypoglycaemia (maintain BSL > 3 mmol/L)
Replacement of bowel may cause sudden rise in IAP → reduced venous return, hypotension, ventilation difficulty, ischaemia of legs
Monitor IAP (proxy: bladder pressure, lower limb perfusion, ventilation parameters) — abandon primary closure if compromised
Staged closure with silo over 7–14 days for large defects
Caudal block for analgesia (single-shot or catheter)
Post-op: ICU ventilated, often delayed extubation
Glycaemic control critical (hypoglycaemia in Beckwith-Wiedemann)

name: Ewing sarcoma resection (limb / pelvic / chest wall)

options: GA + epidural / regional block + arterial line ± CVC
anaesthesia.preferred: GA + appropriate regional + arterial line + CVC for major resection
considerations: Pre-op chemotherapy intense (VDC/IE protocol: vincristine + doxorubicin + cyclophosphamide alternating with ifosfamide + etoposide)
Doxorubicin cardiotoxicity → echo mandatory pre-op
Cyclophosphamide haemorrhagic cystitis (mesna prophylaxis), bone marrow suppression
Ifosfamide encephalopathy + nephrotoxicity (Fanconi syndrome → hypokalaemia, hypophosphataemia)
Pre-op RT possible — fragile tissues, fibrosis
Pelvic Ewing → massive blood loss potential, vascular involvement, ureter at risk
Chest wall Ewing → may need rib resection + reconstruction, pleural opening
Limb-salvage with megaprosthesis — see adult sarcoma considerations
High VTE risk despite paediatric — case by case prophylaxis
ICU post-op for major resection

name: IVC tumour thrombectomy (renal cell / Wilms with caval extension)

options: GA + arterial line + CVC + TEE + CPB-on-standby (Mayo level III/IV)
anaesthesia.preferred: GA + arterial line PRE-induction + CVC + TEE essential + CPB-on-standby (with cardiac surgeon for level III/IV)
considerations: Mayo classification: I (renal vein), II (infrahepatic IVC), III (suprahepatic but infradiaphragmatic), IV (intracardiac)
Level III/IV = potential CPB ± DHCA
TEE essential — track thrombus position, detect embolisation, monitor cardiac function
Tumour fragmentation/embolisation → pulmonary embolism = catastrophic
Massive haemorrhage potential — large IVs × 3, blood ready, MTP active
Liver mobilisation often needed → coagulopathy, blood loss
IVC clamping → reduced preload, hypotension — fluid + vasopressor
Avoid Trendelenburg before clamping (could push thrombus cephalad)
Cell salvage controversial in cancer
Prone-to-supine repositioning sometimes needed
ICU post-op, often delayed extubation, possibly delayed sternal closure
Anticoagulation post-op (heparin → warfarin) for residual cuff

surgerySpecificDrugs.dose: 1 g IV bolus + 1 g/8h infusion (adult) / paed 15 mg/kg + 2 mg/kg/h

options: LA + minimal sedation (preferred for awake patient)
GA only when LA not feasible (risky, last resort)
anaesthesia.preferred: LA infiltration (subxiphoid) + minimal sedation (ketamine 0.25–0.5 mg/kg ± dexmedetomidine 0.2–0.7 mcg/kg/h) + spontaneous ventilation — PATIENT REMAINS AWAKE until pericardium opened
considerations: Reference: BJA Education / O'Connor & Tuman 2010 (Anesth Clin) / Grocott 2011 (CJA)
CRITICAL PRINCIPLE: GA induction in tamponade can cause cardiac arrest — loss of sympathetic compensation + IPPV reduces venous return below the already-fixed-low CO
Tamponade physiology: equalisation of diastolic pressures across all chambers, fixed stroke volume, CO becomes HR-dependent
Pre-induction (BEFORE any sedation): IV access × 2 large-bore, arterial line awake, fluid bolus 500 mL adult / 10–20 mL/kg paed, vasoactive infusions ready (noradrenaline drawn up)
DEFIBRILLATOR PADS APPLIED before induction
Surgeon scrubbed, draped, prepped — ready to incise pericardium IMMEDIATELY if arrest
ALWAYS-AWAKE approach: subxiphoid window under LA + minimal sedation + spontaneous ventilation; this is the safest pathway — convert to GA only AFTER pericardial drainage
MAINTAIN ("fast, full, tight"): HR (no bradycardia), preload (no diuresis, no vasodilators, no nitrates), contractility, SVR
AVOID: drops in any of the above; positive-pressure ventilation before decompression; deep anaesthesia; high-dose propofol; volatile bolus
